summary: Describes the multicast VPN solution designed and deployed by Cisco Systems for BGP/MPLS IP VPNs. It largely overlaps with the IETF framework standardized later and is documented because it was deployed before. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6037 describes how multicast, the one-to-many delivery of IP packets, was carried across a carrier's MPLS-based virtual private networks. The trick is to build one shared path per customer group through the carrier's backbone, so the core routers hold only a small amount of state no matter how many multicast groups the customers use.

questions: what is multicast in bgp mpls ip vpns
what is a default mdt and a data mdt
subtitle: How one vendor carried multicast traffic across a BGP/MPLS IP VPN before the IETF framework for it existed.

tldr.problem: The BGP/MPLS IP VPN specification carries unicast traffic between sites but says nothing about multicast, so a service provider had no standard way to offer multicast inside a customer's VPN.
tldr.mechanism: Multicast traffic from a customer site is encapsulated and sent over a shared distribution tree in the provider backbone, one per group of VPNs, so that the provider's core routers hold state only per VPN rather than per multicast group.
tldr.outcome: The RFC documents the procedures Cisco designed and deployed, most of which are a subset of the framework the IETF later standardized. It is a Historic document, published so that people interoperating with those deployments have a reference.

today: RFC 6037 is a Historic document, published for the record rather than as a standard. The RFC says the procedures it specifies are largely a subset of the generalized MVPN framework the IETF later standardized, and that they differ in some respects because they were deployed first; the unit metadata lists no replacement RFC for it.

sections.title: The Scalability Problem
sections.content:
The base specification for BGP/MPLS IP VPNs gives a VPN optimal unicast routing through the provider's backbone: a packet follows the shortest path as the backbone's own routing algorithm determines it, and the routers in the middle of the backbone, the P routers, hold no routing information about any VPN and no per-VPN state at all.

Optimal multicast routing cannot be had for free. It needs one or more multicast distribution trees in the backbone for each multicast group in use. With source-based trees that means one tree per transmitter of a group; with shared trees it still means one tree per group. Each tree needs state in the P routers along it, and the amount of state is proportional to the number of transmitters.

There has to be at least one tree per group because each group may have a different set of receivers, and multicast routing algorithms go to great lengths to make sure a multicast packet is not sent to a node that is not on the path to a receiver. A provider generally supports many VPNs, each with many multicast groups, and each group with many transmitters, and the provider has no control over those numbers and cannot put a bound on them. One or more trees per group is therefore not scalable.

The solution this document describes keeps the state in the P routers proportional only to the number of VPNs running over the backbone, and makes it insensitive to the number of groups or transmitters inside them. The price is that multicast routing is no longer optimal: a PE that is not on the path to any receiver of a group may still receive its packets and has to discard them. The provider keeps control over that trade-off between optimality and scalability.
sections.plainLanguage: Multicast normally needs a separate delivery tree for every group on the network, and the provider cannot control how many groups its customers create. This design uses one tree per customer instead, so the backbone's cost stays tied to the number of customers rather than to the number of groups they run.

sections.title: Multicast Domains and Shared Trees
sections.content:
A provider decides whether a VPN is multicast-enabled, and if so it corresponds to a Multicast Domain. A PE that attaches to a multicast-enabled VPN belongs to the corresponding domain. For each domain there is a default multicast distribution tree, the Default MDT, through the backbone connecting all the PEs in that domain, including the P routers along the paths. A PE may belong to as many domains as it has VPNs attached, and each domain has its own tree.

The Default MDT is built automatically as the PEs of the domain come up. It does not depend on any multicast traffic existing, so it is there before any traffic is seen. The RFC notes that in the IETF framework these correspond to the inclusive multicast provider shared interfaces, and the per-group trees to the selective ones.

Multicast packets from within a VPN are received from a customer router by an ingress PE, which encapsulates them and, at first, forwards them along the Default MDT to every PE attached to a site of that VPN. Every such PE therefore receives all the multicast packets of the VPN, and a PE that is not on the path to any receiver simply discards the packet. This keeps the customer side unchanged: in BGP/MPLS IP VPNs each customer router is a unicast adjacency of a PE, but customer routers at different sites never become adjacencies of each other, and the same is true for multicast. A customer using PIM-based multicasting can move from a private network to a provider VPN service without changing anything at the customer routers, and any dynamic rendezvous point discovery already in place can stay.

On the provider side, the VPN routing and forwarding table of RFC 4364 is extended to hold multicast routing entries as well, so each VRF has its own multicast routing table. Each PE runs one PIM instance per VRF, called a VPN-specific instance or a PIM C-instance, in which it has a PIM adjacency with each PIM-capable customer router of that VRF. Each PE also runs a provider-wide PIM instance, the PIM P-instance, in which it has a PIM adjacency with its IGP neighbours, the P routers, but not with any customer router. The P routers run the P-instance and no C-instance.

An MD is essentially a set of VRFs whose interfaces can send multicast traffic to each other, and from the point of view of a PIM C-instance it looks like a single multi-access interface. Each MD is configured with a distinct multicast group address in the provider's address space, the Default MDT group address, and the PE routers of the domain become PIM adjacencies of each other over it.
sections.plainLanguage: Customers whose VPNs are allowed to exchange multicast form a group, and the provider builds one shared path across its backbone for that whole group. Every customer site on that path receives every multicast packet, and the ones with no receivers throw them away. The customer side sees no change at all.

sections.title: Building the Tunnels and Finding the Peers
sections.content:
An MD can be seen as a set of PE routers joined by a multicast tunnel. From the point of view of a VPN-specific PIM instance, the tunnel looks like a single multi-access interface, and in the provider's network it is realized as a Default MDT plus zero or more Data MDTs.

An ingress PE is one directly connected to the sender in the VPN, either directly or through a customer router. When the sender starts transmitting, and there are receivers or a rendezvous point behind other PEs in the same domain, the ingress PE becomes the transmitter of either the Default MDT group or a Data MDT group in the provider network. An egress PE is one with a VRF in the domain, and it becomes a receiver of the Default MDT group. It may also join a Data MDT group when it is forwarding traffic for a particular customer group out to an attached site and that group has been associated with that Data MDT. When a packet arrives from a tunnel, the receiving PE derives the domain from the destination address, which is a provider group address, and passes the packet to the matching VRF and PIM instance.

Any of the PIM variants may set up the Default MDT, including sparse mode, bidirectional PIM and source-specific multicast. Except in the source-specific case the PEs need only know the proper group address to begin, because they then discover each other's addresses from the PIM control traffic, such as Hellos, that they receive from one another. With source-specific multicast that does not work, because the trees cannot be built until each PE knows the source address of every other PE in the same domain, so that information has to be discovered separately.

That discovery uses a new BGP address family, the MDT Subsequent Address Family Identifier. Its NLRI holds a route distinguisher, an IPv4 unicast address and a multicast group address. A PE builds one from the IPv4 address it will use as the source of the packets it sends over the tunnel, a route distinguisher assigned to the domain, and the provider group address. When the PE distributes it over BGP it may attach a route target, which must be an import target of every VRF in the domain, so that the ordinary BGP procedures associate the learned addresses with the right VRFs. The encoding is a 12-octet route distinguisher and IPv4 address followed by a 4-octet group address, in BGP messages with AFI 1 and SAFI 66. The RFC requires the use of this address family even when source-specific multicast is not used, and requires that an implementation be able to use it.

Because the tunnel is treated as a LAN interface but no unicast routing runs over it, the RFC also specifies how the reverse path forwarding interface is found for a customer address. When the route for that address in the VRF is a VPN route whose outgoing interface is not one of the VRF's own interfaces, PIM treats the outgoing interface as the tunnel. To find the neighbour, the PE looks up a BGP Connector Attribute distributed with the VPN address, whose value is the address the peer PE uses as the source of its encapsulated packets. In the IETF framework this attribute is replaced by the VRF route import extended community.
sections.plainLanguage: The provider edge routers in a group need to find each other before they can share a path. They do that with a new kind of BGP route that carries the provider group address, plus a route distinguisher that says which customer network it belongs to.

sections.title: Encapsulation in GRE
sections.content:
Multicast traffic is carried through a tree using Generic Routing Encapsulation. The customer's packet, with its own IP header and payload, is placed inside a GRE header, and that in turn inside a new IP header whose destination is the provider group address and whose source is the sending PE's own address.

The IPv4 protocol number in the outer header must be 47. The GRE protocol type must be 0x0800 when the inner header is IPv4 and 0x86dd when it is IPv6. The optional GRE Key field is not needed, because the provider group address in the outer header already identifies the multicast domain and so the VRF context for the payload. The GRE Sequence Number field is also not needed, because the transport layer services for the original application come from the inner IP header. For speed the RFC recommends that the ingress PE encapsulate without setting the checksum, key or sequence number fields.

Because the tunnel destination is a multicast group address, the usual path MTU discovery cannot be used. The ingress PE must not set the Don't Fragment bit in the outer header, and if that bit is clear in the inner header the inner packet should be fragmented before encapsulation if that is appropriate. The RFC says this matters in practice, because reassembly is significantly slower than decapsulating and forwarding on current routers. The TTL of the outer header is left to the local policy of the ingress PE rather than copied from the inner header.

If the provider also offers Internet multicast, the group addresses it uses for its multicast domains must be distinct from the group addresses of those Internet multicasts, which the RFC says is best done with administratively scoped addresses. The customer group addresses need not be distinct from either.
sections.plainLanguage: The customer's multicast packet is wrapped in a new IP header, with the shared path's group address as the destination, and in a GRE header in between. The outer header's Do Not Fragment bit has to be cleared, because the tunnel's destination is a group address and the usual way of learning a path's maximum packet size cannot work.

sections.title: Data MDTs and Their Signalling
sections.content:
The shared tree per domain keeps the state in the core bounded by the number of VPNs, and a single bidirectional tree per VPN scales well as the number of transmitters and receivers grows, but not as the amount of traffic per VPN grows. The routing it provides is also not optimal, since a packet may be forwarded to PE routers that have no receivers for it and have to discard it. When the content is high bandwidth but has only a few receivers, it is worth building a second kind of tree for that traffic alone.

These are called Data MDTs. The ingress PE advertises a different provider group address instead of always using the Default MDT group, and only the PE routers on the path to the eventual receivers join that group, so they form a tree that reaches only the sites that need the traffic. The benefit is less multicast traffic on the backbone and less load on some PEs; the cost is more state in the P routers. The provider has complete control over the trade-off. These trees carry no PIM control traffic, which is why they are called data MDTs.

The signalling is a simple protocol. The PE connected to the source first uses the Default MDT group. When a pre-configured condition is met, commonly that the VPN traffic exceeds a bandwidth threshold, it starts to announce the MDT Join TLV periodically, at the interval of MDT_INTERVAL, to all the PE routers in the domain. The TLV travels in a UDP datagram: over IPv4 for an IPv4 stream, addressed to the all-PIM-routers address 224.0.0.13, and over IPv6 for an IPv6 stream, addressed to ff02::d. The destination UDP port is 3232. The datagram is sent on the Default MDT so that every PE receives it, and any MDT Join that did not arrive over a Default MDT must be dropped.

When a PE connected to a receiver gets the TLV, it joins the announced Data MDT group in the global table. If that group runs in sparse mode or bidirectional PIM the PE builds a shared tree toward the rendezvous point; if it runs in source-specific multicast the PE builds a source tree toward the PE that advertised the TLV, whose address is taken from the source address of the UDP packet that carried it. After the MDT_DATA_DELAY interval the PE at the source starts encapsulating the traffic with the Data MDT group. When the condition no longer holds the source stops announcing the TLV, and if the TLV is not received for longer than MDT_DATA_TIMEOUT the receiving PEs simply leave the Data MDT group in the global instance.

Using Data MDTs needs a set of multicast addresses set aside in advance. With source-specific multicast each domain needs a set and every VRF in it is configured with the same set, so that a set of n addresses lets each PE in the domain be the source of n Data MDTs. Without source-specific multicast each VRF needs its own set, which means reserving far more addresses and complicating operations, so the RFC strongly recommends source-specific multicast for Data MDTs. The MDT Join TLV for an IPv4 stream has type 1 and length 16 and carries the customer source, customer group and provider group as three 32-bit fields; for an IPv6 stream the type is 4 and the length 40, with 128-bit customer source and group fields and a 32-bit provider group.
sections.plainLanguage: When one flow is worth the trouble, the sending site announces a second, private path for it, and only the sites with receivers join that path. The announcement is a small message sent in UDP to a fixed port, repeated on a timer, and it stops once the flow stops.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC does not set out new security analysis of its own. It points at three existing documents. RFC 4364 discusses the security considerations that apply when that kind of VPN is deployed. The sparse mode PIM specification discusses the considerations that pertain to the use of PIM. And the considerations of RFC 4023 and RFC 4797 apply whenever VPN traffic is carried through IP or GRE tunnels, which is exactly what this document specifies.
sections.plainLanguage: This document adds no security analysis of its own. It says to follow the guidance for VPNs, for the multicast routing protocol, and for tunnelled traffic.

cells: PIM control traffic and, by default, the VPN's data traffic
Every PE in the multicast domain
Only the PEs on the path to receivers
Automatically as the PEs of the domain come up
Signalled by the source with an MDT Join TLV
Bounded by the number of VPNs
Higher, because each Data MDT adds state

viz.caption: GRE ENCAPSULATION OF A VPN MULTICAST PACKET
THE MDT JOIN TLV PORT AND TIMERS

items.label: UDP port
items.desc: The destination UDP port of the datagram carrying the MDT Join TLV.

items.label: MDT_INTERVAL
items.desc: How often the source PE repeats the MDT Join TLV. Default 60 seconds.

items.label: MDT_DATA_DELAY
items.desc: How long the source PE waits before it starts using the Data MDT group. Default 3 seconds.

items.label: MDT_DATA_TIMEOUT
items.desc: How long the receiving PEs wait without hearing a Join TLV before leaving the Data MDT group. Default 3 minutes.

items.label: MDT_DATA_HOLDDOWN
items.desc: How long the source PE stays on the Data MDT group, to avoid oscillation on bursty traffic. Default 1 minute.
